title: The House Bunny
full_review:
To judge by "The House Bunny" (Columbia/Relativity), life at the Playboy mansion is one long idyll of largely innocent fun, presided over by the magazine's founder, a by-now-avuncular Hugh Hefner, who makes a cameo appearance portraying himself. So when ditzy but kindhearted Shelley Darlingson (Anna Faris), a mid-20s model whose highest ambition is to be featured as a centerfold, is abruptly exiled from her room there, the film pitches her plight as little short of paradise lost.

After attempting to live in her beat-up station wagon and spending a night in jail, Shelley wanders onto a local campus and into a snooty sorority, an establishment she immediately volunteers to join on the grounds of its supposed similarities with Hefner's domain. Although rebuffed, she's advised to try the Zeta house, whose seven remaining denizens are such misfits and social outcasts that they may accept even the likes of her.

This dwindling band is led by smart but eccentric Natalie (Emma Stone), who immediately senses Shelley's potential and convinces her doubtful sisters (Kat Dennings, Katharine McPhee and Rumer Willis, among others) to make the new arrival their house mother. Since the chapter is under threat of being shuttered unless 30 new pledges enroll within a short time, the irrepressible Shelley immediately sets to work helping the Zetas reinvent themselves as popular party girls with whom everyone on campus will want to associate.

Her only distraction from this crusade is the sensitive administrator of a nearby nursing home (Colin Hanks) with whom she's smitten, but whose depth of character confuses her.

 

Despite its free pass to the Playboy lifestyle, director Fred Wolf's comedy ultimately asserts the value of substance over appearance, and its central romantic relationships are quite traditional. Though the weaknesses in co-writers Karen McCullah Lutz and Kirsten Smith's script become uncomfortably apparent well before Shelley finds herself in the inevitable "neither fish nor fowl" dilemma, both Faris and Stone remain game and their partnership provides the film's comic core.

The film contains brief rear nudity, much sexual humor, one use of the f-word, some crude and crass language, and an out-of-wedlock pregnancy. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
